Oxygen-limited aeration for relieving the impact of phenolic
compounds in anaerobic treatment of coal gasiﬁcation wastewater
Wei Wang*, Jing Zhang, Shun Wang, Jun Shen, Shang-Lei Pan
Department of Municipal Engineering, School of Civil and Hydraulic Engineering, Hefei University of Technology, Hefei 230009, China
a r t i c l e
i n f o
Article history:
Received 2 November 2013
Received in revised form
14 June 2014
Accepted 15 June 2014
Available online 2 July 2014
Keywords:
Coal gasiﬁcation wastewater
Anaerobic
Expanded-bed GAC reactor
Oxygen-limited aeration
Impact
a b s t r a c t
Anaerobic digestion is an efﬁcient tool for improving aerobic biodegradability of coal gasiﬁcation
wastewater, but the shock loading usually results in a failed performance of the anaerobic process. The
oxygen-limited aeration was conducted to handle the impact of coal gasiﬁcation wastewater in an
anaerobic expanded-bed GAC reactor. Results indicated that the oxygen-limited aeration of 0e0.5 mgO2/
L could shorten the recovery time from 23 to 11 days under natural condition, and the addition of 1 g/L
PAC could reduce the recovery time to 14 days. The corresponding removal efﬁciencies of COD and
phenolic compounds could increase to above 60 and 50%, respectively. The phenol utilization rates of
sludge reached 83.9 ± 5.7 mg phenol/(g VSS d) after recovery of reactor performance by using oxygen-
limited aeration, and only 70.4 ± 3.8 mg phenol/(g VSS d) by using natural recovery and 65.2 ± 5.9 mg
phenol/(g VSS d) by using PAC addition. The recovery strategy of oxygen-limited aeration might be
helpful to relieve the inhibitory effect of phenolic compounds and restore metabolic activity of anaerobic
bacteria.

1. Introduction
At present, in China, coal syngas is produced in large quantities
to meet the requirement of natural gas and to provide the raw
materials in the manufacture of chemical products, such as meth-
anol, synthetic ammonia and oleﬁn (Chen and Xu, 2010; Yoon and
Lee, 2012). However, the difﬁculties in treatment of coal gasiﬁcation
wastewater (CGW) are far beyond the imagination. The CGW con-
tained phenolic compounds, heterocyclic and polycyclic aromatic
hydrocarbons, long chain alkanes, ammonia, thiocyanate, and cy-
anide (Sharma et al., 2012). Among these compounds, phenolic
compounds were the main organic pollutants and contributed
about 30e60% of the COD content (Wang et al., 2010). Especially,
the concentration of total phenols was still around 400 mg/L even
though the pretreatment of solvent extraction (Gai et al., 2008; Yu
et al., 2010). The toxicity and recalcitrance of phenolic compounds
inhibited its biological degradation. Generally, the CGW was treated
using anoxiceoxic process or conventional activated sludge pro-
cess, because the most of phenolic compounds could be degraded
readily under aerobic conditions (Li et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2011a,b).
However, the aerobic biological treatment could not reduce the
concentrations of COD and phenolic compounds in the CGW to
meet the national emission standards.
Many attentions had paid to anaerobic biological technologies in
the treatment of CGW because of their advantages, which included
low energy consumption, detoxiﬁcation and improvement of
biodegradability (Fox et al., 1990; Nakhla et al., 1990; Wang et al.,
2011). In the 1980s of last century, anaerobic activated carbon ﬁl-
ter was used to treat the CGW, while excellent removal efﬁciency of
organic matter was achieved by a combination of anaerobic
fermentation and adsorption (Suidan et al., 1983). Operational
techniques using expanded-bed or ﬂuidized-bed anaerobic gran-
ular activated carbon (GAC) bioreactors were developed subse-
quently for reducing the cost in treating the CGW (Pfeffer and
Suidan, 1989; Fox et al., 1990; Nakhla et al., 1990). Because of the
toxicity of CGW, the full strength wastewater was not treatable at
organic loading rates (OLR) above 10 kg COD/(m3 d) while the GAC
reactors treating the diluted wastewater could achieve around 90%
removal of COD and over 99.5% reduction of phenolic compounds at
OLR range of 32e34 kg COD/(m3 d) in the synthetic CGW (Nakhla
and Suidan, 1995). Furthermore, the periodic partial replacement
of GAC was also an effective way to overcome the toxicity of the
wastewater in the anaerobic GAC reactors (Pfeffer and Suidan,
1989; Nakhla et al., 1990). Except the anaerobic GAC technologies,
anaerobic treatment of actual CGW was investigated in the con-
ventional anaerobic processes, such as two-continuous UASB

reactors and addition of PAC in the UASB reactor (Wang et al., 2011;
Wang and Han, 2012). These results demonstrated that anaerobic
digestion had a signiﬁcant improvement effect on the biodegrad-
ability of CGW, but the COD removal exceeding 70% was difﬁcult at
OLR range of 2.5e3.0 kg COD/(m3 d) in the absence of activated
carbon. Obviously, anaerobic expended-bed GAC (EB-GAC) reactor
was more efﬁcient than the conventional anaerobic processes for
treating the actual CGW.
In fact, the composition of actual CGW was complicated and
varied from one gasiﬁcation plant to another, depending on the
quality of raw coal, gasiﬁer types, gasiﬁcation temperature, and
recovery methods of byproducts. So, the application of anaerobic
processes in the treatment of CGW had been hampered by a lack of
understanding of factors associated with process stability, such as
shock loading and recovery methods. In the anaerobic GAC reactors,
one method using the periodic partial replacement of GAC had been
successfully applied for reducing the toxicity and enhancing the
stability in the laboratory studies (Nakhla et al., 1990). However, on
an industrial scale, the shock loading appeared frequently in the
inﬂuent, and the periodic partial replacement of large volumes of
GAC was unreasonable and very costly.
The aim of this study was to investigate the effect of oxygen-
limited aeration and addition of powdered activated carbon (PAC)
on the recovery process of anaerobic EB-GAC reactor treating CGW
after shock loading. The start-up of the anaerobic EB-GAC reactor
was recorded and the impact of shock loading was evaluated on the
operation of the EB-GAC reactor. Comparing with the natural re-
covery, the recovery process and the mechanism of oxygen-limited
aeration and addition of PAC were analyzed.
2. Material and methods
2.1. Experimental setup and inoculum
The EB-GAC reactor was constructed of cylindrical plexiglass
column with an internal diameter of 5 cm and a working volume of
1 L. A supporting layer was placed at the bottom of the reactor to
support the GAC and distribute inﬂuent wastewater and air. The
temperature was maintained at 35 ± 2 C by a constant temperature
controller through electric heating. The reactor was initially charged
with 100 g of 16  20 mesh GAC. An internal recycle wastewater of
0.2 L/minprovided an initial expansion of GAC bed in the reactor. The
seed sludge was obtained from a full-scale anaerobic reactor at a
CGW treatment plant in the northeast region of China. The initial
suspended solids (SS) and volatile suspended solids (VSS) added to
the reactor were around 10.5 and 7.1 g/L, respectively.
2.2. Wastewater characteristics and GC-MS analysis

cated composition and the wastewater characteristics with their

COD (2023 ± 146), BOD5 (685 ± 47), phenolic compounds
(392 ± 35), volatile fatty acids (759 ± 84), ammonia nitrogen
(129 ± 10), oil (45 ± 6), thiocyanate (65 ± 7) and pH (7.5 ± 0.3). The
macro- and micro-nutrients were added to the anaerobic EB-GAC
reactor as described in the early work (Wang et al., 2010).
2.3. Start-up and operation
The operational schedule of the EB-GAC reactor was divided into
four phases: start-up, natural recovery, addition of PAC, and
oxygen-limited aeration. Normal operation of the EB-GAC reactor
was maintained at COD and phenolic concentrations of around
2000 and 400 mg/L at a HRT of 24 h. The ﬁrst phase lasted for 156
days during the start-up period. For the second period extending to
day 194, the organic loading on the EB-GAC reactor was maintained
at 5.16 kg COD/(m3 d) with 24 h between days 157 and 158, while
the concentrations of COD and phenolic compounds increased from
1859 and 354.5 mg/L to 5160 and 815 mg/L respectively in the
inﬂuent. The anaerobic EB-GAC reactor was allowed to recover fully
from the shock loading and the recovery time was deﬁned as the
time between the initiation of recovery action and the time when
the removal efﬁciency of phenolic compounds achieved above 50%.
After the natural recovery of reactor performance, the EB-GAC
reactor was continuously operated at a pseudo-steady state for
two weeks. Between days 195 and 196, the shock loading of 5.32 kg
COD/(m3 d) was exerted on the EB-GAC reactor for one day time.1 g

days 196 to 199 and then the reactor performance was gradually
recovered without the addition of PAC. For the fourth period, the
organic loading rate of 5.46 kg COD/(m3 d) and phenolic loading
rate of 0.85 kg/(m3 d) in the EB-GAC reactor were maintained for
24 h between days 224 and 225. The oxygen-limited aeration of
0e0.5 mg/L was used to the recovery of the reactor performance for
3 days, and then the EB-GAC reactor performance was gradually
recovered without aeration on day 227.
2.4. Analytical methods
COD, BOD5, SS, VSS, phenols, oil, thiocyanate, and ammonia ni-
trogen were determined according to Standard Methods (Wei et al.,
2002). pH values were analyzed by a pH meter (pHS-3C, Leici,
China). Volatile fatty acids (VFAs) were analyzed by the distillation
method (Anderson and Yang, 1992). The biogas production of the
reactor was detected by the gas ﬂowmeter. Methane content of the
biogas was measured using a liquid displacement system with a
3 mol/L NaOH solution. Phenol utilization rate (PUR) tests were
used to evaluate the metabolic activity of the biomass for degrading
phenol before and after the shock loading in the EB-GAC reactor
(Wang et al., 2010). For organic composition, the inﬂuent was
analyzed via GC-MS and the analytical conditions were described in
the previous paper (Wang et al., 2002). The morphology of the
sludge samples was analyzed using a scanning electron microscope
(SEM, S-4700, HITACHI).
3. Results
3.1. Start-up of the EB-GAC reactor
The removal efﬁciencies of COD and phenolic compounds dur-
ing the start-up period in the EB-GAC reactor are shown in Fig. 2.
For the ﬁrst four days, both the removal efﬁciencies of COD and
phenolic compounds were above 75%, but subsequently the
removal efﬁciencies decreased quickly to below 15% after day 7.
Obviously, the adsorption capacity of GAC was exhausted and the
phenolic compounds almost penetrated the EB-GAC reactor. With
the inﬂuent COD and phenolic compounds of around 2006 and
401 mg/L, the concentrations of COD and phenolic compounds
were still above 1000 and 300 mg/L in the efﬂuent even after
another 70 days' operation, and the corresponding removal efﬁ-
ciencies of COD and phenolic compounds were mostly below 45
and 20%, respectively. Although the seed sludge had been accli-
mated to the CGW for a long time under methanogenic conditions,
the sludge still needed sufﬁcient time to adapt the environment in
the EB-GAC reactor. At this stage, the maximum production of
methane was only about 10 mL and no methane production was
detected at the most of time. This indicated that the methanogenic
organisms were being affected by the toxic substances in the
inﬂuent. At the end of the start-up period (from days 143 to 156),
the removal efﬁciencies of COD and phenolic compounds remained
at around 69 and 52%, and the concentrations of COD and phenolic
compounds decreased to around 613 and 195 mg/L, respectively.
3.2. Natural recovery of the EB-GAC reactor after the shock loading
On day 157, the inﬂuent COD concentration was increased from
1859 to 5160 mg/L with an increase in the concentration of phenolic
compounds from354.5 to 815 mg/L, while keeping this state for 24h.
Results of the shock loading and natural recovery of the EB-GAC
reactor are illustrated in Fig. 3. In the initial days (days 158e159),
the concentrations of efﬂuent COD and phenolic compounds sud-
denly rose to exceed the inﬂuent concentrations due to the residual
organic contaminants and the increase in efﬂuent suspended solids.
The recovery process was slow from days 163 to 180, and the
removal efﬁciencies of COD and phenolic compounds were around
63 and 53% respectively on day 180. The whole time lasted 23 days
for the recovery process of the reactor performance. Subsequently,

3.3. Recovery after the shock loading by addition of PAC in the EB-
GAC reactor
On day 195 of reactor operation, the COD concentrations were
increased from 2065 to 5320 mg/L, and the concentration of
phenolic compounds increased from 379.6 to 795.7 mg/L. Results of
addition of PAC for tackling the shock loading in the EB-GAC reactor
are shown in Fig. 4. These changes caused a decrease in COD
removal from 70.7 to 6.9% in one day time. In order to shorten the
recovery time of reactor performance, 1 g/L of PAC was added into
the reactor for adsorbing the pollutants in the inﬂuent from days
196 to 198, which reduced the concentrations of COD and phenolic
compounds to 1427.5 and 248.2 mg/L respectively in the efﬂuent.
This resulted in a signiﬁcant improvement in treatment efﬁciency
of the anaerobic EB-GAC reactor. Within the next 11 days, the
removal efﬁciencies of COD and phenolic compounds increased to
62.7 and 50.3%, respectively. The recovery time was 14 days after
the shock loading in the EB-GAC reactor. To improve the reactor
performance, the EB-GAC reactor was continued with two weeks'
operation. On day 223, the removal efﬁciencies of COD and phenolic
compounds were 70 and 50.6% and the corresponding concentra-
tions were 574.8 and 219.8 mg/L respectively in the efﬂuent.
3.4. Recovery after the shock loading by oxygen-limited aeration in
the EB-GAC reactor
Results of oxygen-limited aeration for tackling the shock loading
in the EB-GAC reactor are shown in Fig. 5. On day 224, the shock
loading was provided with COD of 5460 mg/L and phenolic com-
pounds of 850 mg/L, and the removal efﬁciencies of COD and
phenolic compounds decreased from 70 and 50.6% to 4.2 and 3.9%,
respectively. The oxygen-limited aeration of 0e0.5 mgO2/L as a
recovery strategy was used to accelerate the recovery of reactor
performance for 3 days. The efﬂuent concentrations of COD and
phenolic compounds were 757 and 129.4 mg/L, respectively on day
227. On day 228, the removal efﬁciencies of COD and phenolic
compounds quickly decreased to 35.2 and 25.8% due to the stop of
oxygen-limited aeration. Subsequently, the gradual increase of
removal efﬁciencies was observed in the next 7 days. The removal
efﬁciencies of COD and phenolic compounds were 62.5 and 51.6%,
respectively on day 235. As calculated, the recovery time was 11
days after the third shock loading in the EB-GAC reactor. For the
next 16 days the inﬂuent concentrations of COD and phenolic

3.5. Phenol utilization rate tests
PUR tests evaluated the metabolic activities of suspended sludge
for degrading phenol in the EB-GAC reactor during the different
periods, as shown in Table 1. At the end of the start-up period, the
PUR values increased from the initial values of 35.6 ± 5.2 mg
phenol/(g VSS d) in the seed sludge to 63.1 ± 7.4 mg phenol/
(g VSS d) in the suspended sludge on day 155. When the shock
loading happened, the SUR decreased to 43.5 ± 6.0 mg phenol/
(g VSS d) on day 160 and recovered to 70.4 ± 3.8 mg phenol/
(g VSS d) after the natural recovery on day 193. On day 198, the SUR
values reduced to 41.4 ± 3.5 mg phenol/(g VSS d) due to the second
shock loading. After the recovery with addition of PAC, the SUR
values recovered to 65.2 ± 5.9 mg phenol/(g VSS d). When the third

3.6. Morphology of the sludge
Fig. 6 shows the photomicrographs from a SEM analysis of the
suspended sludge in the reactor and the bioﬁlm on the GAC par-
ticles thus indicating that the PAC acted as a support for bioﬁlm
growth. The sludge was mainly comprised of short-rod type bac-
teria (Fig. 6a and b). The photomicrographs showed the dominance
of short-rod type bacteria embedded by a thick layer of extracel-
lular polymeric substances (EPS) (Fig. 6a). It was reported that a
mass of EPS would be produced when the anaerobic sludge suffered
from toxic environment (Aquino and Stuckey, 2004). On the basis of
appearance, the biomass in the reactor was mainly composed of
acidogenic-like bacteria and the predominant bacteria which were
similar from that of bioﬁlm in GAC surface.
4. Discussion
According to the previous studies, anaerobic digestion plays a
positive role in the biological treatment of coal gasiﬁcation waste-
water (Wang et al., 2011). With the inﬂuent COD and phenolic
compounds of around 2000 and 400 mg/L, the maximum removal
efﬁciencies can reach above 70 and 50% respectively at the HRT of
24 h in the EB-GAC reactor. Researchers have reported that suc-
cessful operation of the anaerobic GAC system requires a carbon
replacement schedule to be maintained, which can keep the bulk
concentrations of toxic compounds below their toxic threshold
(Nakhla et al., 1990). Before the shock loading, efﬁcient COD
removal and phenolic degradation were achieved in the EB-GAC
reactor,
which
conﬁrmed
the
feasibility
of
this
wastewater
treatment approach. However, due to the inability to timely
replacement of GAC, the EB-GAC reactor would also run to failure
once the shock loading impacted and the recovery time was long
without any measures. So, the instability of the EB-GAC reactor was
still the most disadvantages for its application in the treatment of
CGW.
As known, as long as the toxic substances can be absorbed by the
activated carbon, they would not inhibit the anaerobic bacteria. But,
the adsorption capacity of GAC or PAC was very low for the actual
CGW due to its high concentration and complex composition. If
there were high concentrations of toxic compounds in the inﬂuent,
the recovery strategies should reduce these toxic compounds to the
concentrations below their threshold levels. Previous works had
indicated that addition of PAC and oxygen-limited aeration was the
best recovery strategies in the UASB reactor (Wang and Han, 2012).
Also, in the EB-GAC reactor, addition of PAC of 1 g/L shortened the
recovery time from 23 to 14 days and oxygen-limited aeration of
0e0.5 mgO2/L reduced the recovery time to 11 days. Obviously,
these two recovery strategies could shorten the recovery time after
shock loading, especially oxygen-limited aeration. In fact, the
limited aeration had been employed as an efﬁcient way to achieve
high treatment efﬁciency under anaerobic conditions (Zitomer and
Shrout, 1998; Zhou et al., 2007; Xu et al., 2014). The recovery
strategy of oxygen-limited aeration was more suitable for the EB-
GAC reactor than the UASB reactor, which the aeration didn't
result a huge loss of sludge in the EB-GAC reactor.
Phenolic compounds didn't accumulate in the EB-GAC reactor
when the GAC attained adsorption saturation. When the bacteria
utilized the phenolic compounds that adsorbed by the GAC, the
biological GAC reactor might played an important role in degra-
dation of phenolic compounds. After the shock loading, the high
concentration of phenolic compounds not only caused rapid
depletion of adsorption capacity of GAC, but also inhibited seriously
the activity of anaerobic sludge. Addition of PAC could reduce the
bioavailable concentration of phenolic compounds to tackle the
shock loading, but the recovery rate of the activity of anaerobic
sludge was relatively slow. It was noteworthy that oxygen-limited
aeration could effectively reduce the residual concentration of
phenolic compounds and also could quickly recover the activity of
anaerobic sludge. The degradation rates of phenolic compounds
under oxygen-limited condition were higher than the values under
anaerobic condition. In the traditional sense, the methanogenic
microbes were sensitive to toxic pollutants. However, the metabolic
activity of anaerobic sludge wasn't inhibited completely by the
emergence of molecular oxygen (Zitomer and Shrout, 1998). After

the recovery strategy of oxygen-limited aeration, the methane
production was still observed with a short-term adaption, the total
gas production was lower than expected values from the theoret-
ical calculation. So, it was speculated that the anaerobic microor-
ganisms were mainly composed of facultative bacteria in the EB-
GAC reactor. In addition, the EPS was considered to be a defensive
strategy to protect microbes against shock loadings caused by toxic
compounds, because the concentration of toxic compounds in the
extracellular was generally lower than in the intracellular due to
the diffusion effects. Comparing with addition of PAC, the recovery
strategy of oxygen-limited aeration might be helpful to relieve the
inhibition caused by toxic pollutants and restore the metabolic
activity of anaerobic microbes. Thus, oxygen-limited aeration was a
promising strategy to handle the shock loading in anaerobic
treatment of CGW. It was suggested that the potential application of
this strategy was suitable for anaerobic treatment of CGW. Further
research is required to establish the optimum conditions of re-
covery strategies.
5. Conclusion
The EB-GAC process provided an efﬁcient technique for anaer-
obic treatment of coal gasiﬁcation wastewater, but the shock
loading of around 5.2 kg COD/(m3 d) would result in a failed per-
formance. The PAC addition and oxygen-limited aeration could
shorten the recovery time from 23 days under natural condition to
14 and 11 days, respectively. As compared to addition of PAC, the
oxygen-limited aeration might be helpful to reduce microbial in-
hibition caused by toxic pollutants and restore metabolic activity of
anaerobic bacteria. The oxygen-limited aeration was a promising
strategy to handle the shock loading in anaerobic treatment of
CGW.
